newsitem.title: UK: Metals end mixed as LME advances falter.
newsitem.headline: Metals end mixed as LME advances falter.

text.p: Base metals opted not to extend gains sustained earlier this week during Friday LME trading, with copper and aluminium settling back to lower closes.
Both copper and aluminium found overhead resistance levels difficult to overcome, despite some positive inventory data, while other metals eased from initial highs to end mixed.
"They've (copper/aluminium) had a good run this week, so there was a bit of profit-taking and booksquaring around. We're still looking for higher numbers next week," one trader said.
Copper stalled at $2,270 soon after an unexpected LME warehouse stock fall of 3,425 tonnes, and prices spent most of the session fluctuating between $2,250 and $2,260.
Overhead, there is resistance around $2,280 and then $2,313, while the support is expected from $2,250 down to $2,200.
Traders expect further short-term gains, based on tight nearby spreads around Jan/Feb dates, with European physical tightness also supportive.
Last three months business was at $2,255 a tonne, down $15 from Thursday. The cash/threes backwardation ended at $150/155.
Aluminium lost ground in line with copper's trend, but should be helped by constructive producer stock data as reported by the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) for November.
Producer stocks fell 33,000 tonnes to 1.653 million tonnes. the lowest since November 1992, while fabricated inventories of 1.437 million tonnes is the lowest for over 15 years.
Analyst Nick Moore of the Flemings Global Mining Group noted that although there has been an element of re-distribution producer stocks have fallen more than LME inventories have risen recently.
"It (the data) not only supports current prices, but it opens the door for better prices as the hedge funds move in," he said.
Prices again met some producer selling above $1,600 today, and eased back to close at $1,596, down $14.

The cash/threes spread in the alloy market continued to narrow, reflecting good physical demand and falling stocks, touching level/$5 contango at one point. Three months prices held steady, closing at $1,510/12 a tonne.
Lead pushed higher, helped by expectations cold weather in Europe will impact on replacement battery demand, and last business was at $698, up $6.
However, zinc faltered at $1,070 resistance, despite a solid 3,700-tonne inventory fall, and the market ended at $1,064, up just $1.
Nickel was erratic, with gains prompted by a 678-tonne stock fall lacking followthrough, although the market was well supported on dips. Last trade was just $10 lower at $7,200.
The quiet tin market finished at $5,860, up just $5.
